{{Short description|Japanese god}} {{Infobox deity | type = Japanese | name = Moriya-no-Kami
(Moriya) | image = Moriya Shrine - 洩矢神社 社殿.jpg | caption = Moriya Shrine in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Nagano Prefecture]] | god_of = Indigenous ''[[kami]]'' of the [[Lake Suwa]] area | script_name = Japanese | script = 洩矢神, 守矢神, 守屋神, 守宅神 | other_names = Moriya (Moreya)-no-Ōkami (洩矢大神)
Moriya Daimyōjin (守屋大明神)
Moriya Daijin (守屋大臣)
Moriya no Akuzoku (洩矢の悪賊) | cult_center = [[:ja:洩矢神社|Moriya Shrine]] | children = [[:ja:守宅神|Moriya]] / Morita (son; ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'')
Tamaru-hime (daughter; ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'')
[[:ja:千鹿頭神|Chikatō]] (son; local legend) | texts = ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'', ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'', ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' }} '''Moreya''' or '''Moriya''' (洩矢神, ''Moriya- / Moriya'') is a Japanese [[Kami|god]] who appears in various myths and legends of the [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] region in [[Nagano Prefecture]] (historical [[Shinano Province]]). The most famous of such stories is that of his battle against [[Takeminakata]], the god of the [[Suwa-taisha|Grand Shrine of Suwa]] (''Suwa Taisha''). Moriya is regarded as the mythical ancestor of the Moriya clan (守矢氏), a priestly family that formerly served in the Upper Suwa Shrine (上社, ''Kamisha''), one of the two sub-shrines that make up Suwa Taisha. In addition, he is venerated as a local tutelary deity (''[[Ujigami|ubusunagami]]'') in a shrine in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]] near the [[Tenryū River]], which in later variants of the aforementioned myth is identified as the place where Takeminakata and Moriya fought each other. Local historians have long interpreted the story of the conflict between the two deities as the mythicization of a historical event in which a powerful local clan that ruled the [[Lake Suwa]] region and its vicinity (identified with the Moriya) was defeated by invaders who wrested control of the area (identified in turn with the [[Suwa clan]], the high priestly lineage of the Upper Suwa Shrine that claimed to be Takeminakata's descendants), although a number of scholars have recently argued that it may actually be of later origin, heavily influenced by or outright based on medieval legends concerning [[Soga–Mononobe conflict|the conflict]] between [[Prince Shōtoku]] and the anti-Buddhist ''[[Muraji|ōmuraji]]'' [[Mononobe no Moriya]], who may have been the inspiration for the god's name. ==Name== What is currently the most commonly used rendering of Moriya's name in [[kanji]], 洩矢, appear in sources such as the ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'' (1356) and the genealogical record of the Moriya family compiled during the early [[Meiji period]] (late 19th century) known as the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜, "Genealogy of the ''Jinchō'' Moriya clan"). It is also the rendering adopted by Moriya Shrine ([[:ja:洩矢神社|洩矢神社]]) in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]] in Nagano, where the deity is enshrined.{{cite web|url=https://moriyajinja.amebaownd.com/|title=Moriya Shrine Official Website (洩矢神社公式HP)}} A number of other texts (see below) meanwhile refer to the god as ''Moriya Daijin'' (守屋大臣), an epithet more often used for the historical Mononobe no Moriya in medieval and later sources.''Nihon Kōtei Keizu'' (日本皇帝系図), in {{cite book|editor1=Hanawa Hokiichi|title=群書系図部集 第二 (Gunsho keizubushū, vol. 2)|date=1973|publisher=Zoku Gunsho-ruijū Kanseikai|page=51|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dxv_wsnc14YC&pg=RA1-PA19|isbn=9784797102741}}{{cite book|last1=Dickson|first1=Walter G.|title=Gleanings from Japan|date=1889|publisher=W. Blackwood and Sons|page=[https://archive.org/details/gleaningsfromja01dickgoog/page/n370 360]|url=https://archive.org/details/gleaningsfromja01dickgoog}}{{cite book|last1=Arai|first1=Hakuseki|translator=Joly, Henri L. |translator2=Inada, Hogitarō|title=The Sword Book in Honchō Gunkikō and the Book of Samé Ko Hi Sei Gi of Inaba Tsurio|date=1963|publisher=Charles E. Tuttle|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JWceAAAAIAAJ&q=moriya+daijin|page=14}} ==Background== ===Suwa Shrine and its priesthood=== [[File:Suwa-taisha, Kamisha Honmiya, haiden-2.jpg|thumb|312x312px|The Upper Shrine of Suwa's Main Shrine (上社本宮, ''Kamisha Honmiya''), located in [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]]] The Grand Shrine of Suwa (''Suwa Taisha'') in [[Nagano Prefecture]] consists of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine (上社, ''Kamisha''), located southeast of [[Lake Suwa]], in the cities of [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino]] and [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine (下社, ''Shimosha''), located in the town of [[Shimosuwa]] in the northern side of the lake. Historically, the Upper and Lower Suwa Shrines essentially functioned as two separate entities, each with its own set of shrines, religious ceremonies, and priests. Before the rise of [[State Shinto]] in the [[Meiji period]], the position of head priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝) in the Upper Shrine was occupied by members of the [[Suwa clan]] (諏訪氏, ''Suwa-shi''), also known as the Miwa or Jin (神氏, ''Jinshi'' / ''Miwa-shi''). The Suwa traditionally traced its lineage back to the shrine's deity [[Takeminakata]], who is also known as Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]] (諏訪大明神), the "Great Deity of Suwa." For a long time, the occupant of the high priestly office was revered as a god in the flesh (''[[arahitogami]]''), the living incarnation or "body" (''[[shintai]]'') of Suwa Daimyōjin.{{sfnp|Ihara|2008|pp=157–185}}{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|pp=2-3}}{{sfnp|Inoue|2003|pp=356-357}} The second-highest office was that of the ''Kan-no-Osa'' or ''Jinchō'' (神長), later known as the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官). This priest officiated the Upper Shrine's ceremonies, including the ''Ōhōri'''s investiture ceremony, which accorded him a preeminent status in the hierarchy. He also had the prerogative of summoning and inhering the [[Mishaguji]], divine spirits who figure in some of the shrine's religious rites, onto objects who will serve as their vessels (''[[yorishiro]]'') for the duration of these rituals and then dismissing them at their conclusion.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|pp=4-5}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|pp=25-27}} The hereditary occupants of this office were members of a clan called Moriya (守矢氏, ''Moriya-shi''), who claimed to have descended from a certain local god named Moriya or Moreya, who had been subjugated by Takeminakata.{{sfnp|Inoue|2003|pp=356-357}} ==Mythology== ===Moriya and Suwa Daimyōjin=== The most famous story involving Moriya is that of his battle against Takeminakata / Suwa Daimyōjin, who is said to have come to the Suwa region seeking to dwell there or to conquer it. One version of this myth involves the Suwa deity or his subordinate defeating Moriya, described as armed with a certain kind of iron weapon or implement, using only a [[wisteria]] (藤, ''fuji'') branch or vine.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|pp=2-3}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|p=21}}{{sfnp|Oh|2011|pp=157-158}}{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|pp=24-25}} Another variant has Suwa Daimyōjin facing and defeating Moriya on the battlefield. ==== "Moriya the evil outlaw" in the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' ==== [[File:Fujishima Shrine (Nakasu, Suwa) - 藤島社（諏訪市中洲）- 2.jpg|thumb|353x353px|Fujishima Shrine (藤島社) in Nakasu, Suwa, one of the Upper Shrine of Suwa's [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrines]]]] What is perhaps the most well-known version of the story is found in the 1356 text ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'', where it is recorded as the [[origin myth]] of Fujishima Shrine (藤島社, ''Fujishima-sha'') in [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]], one of the Upper Shrine's [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrines]] where its yearly rice-planting ceremony is traditionally held.{{sfnp|Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|1995|pp=681-683}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|pp=88-91}} {{Quote|Regarding the god of Fujishima [Shrine] (藤島の明神, ''Fujishima no Myōjin''): when the revered deity (尊神, ''sonjin'', i.e. Suwa Daimyōjin) [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] long ago, Moriya the evil outlaw (洩矢の惡賊, ''Moriya no akuzoku''), seeking to hinder him, took up an iron ring (鐵輪) to fight him, but the [Fujishima] deity picked up a wisteria branch and defeated [Moriya]. Finally, he brought down heresy (邪輪, ''jarin'', lit. "ring/wheel/circle of evil") and held up [[:en:Dharma (Buddhism)|the true Dharma]] (正法, ''shōbō''). When the god swore an oath and threw the wisteria branch away, immediately it took root [in the ground], its branches and leaves flourishing in abundance, and [sprouted] beautiful blossoms, leaving behind a marker of the battleground for posterity. This is the reason why the Fujishima deity is named thus.{{efn|「抑コノ藤嶋ノ明神ト申ハ、尊神垂迹ノ昔、洩矢ノ惡賊神居ヲサマタケントセシ時、洩矢ハ鐵輪ヲ持シテアラソヒ、明神ハ藤枝ヲトリテ是ヲ伏シ給フ。ツイニ邪輪ヲ降シテ正法ヲ興ス。 明神誓ヲ發テ、藤枝ヲナケ給シカハ、則根ヲサシテ枝葉ヲサカヘ、花蘂アサヤカニシテ、戰場ノシルシヲ萬代ニ殘ス。藤嶋ノ明神ト号スル此ユヘナリ。」}}{{sfnp|Kanai|1982|p=252}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=151-152}}}} The myth is also found in a [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinto-Buddhist]] liturgical eulogy (講式, ''kōshiki'') to the Suwa deity, the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki'' (諏方大明神講式), thought to have been composed by the ''Ekotoba'''s author, Suwa (Kosaka) Enchū (1295-1364{{sfnp|Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|1995|p=814}}), around the same time as the former text.{{cite web|title=諏方大明神講式|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=KSRM-287105|website=National Institute of Japanese Literature (国文学研究資料館)}}{{sfnp|Shintō Taikei Hensankai|1982|pp=9, 237ff.}}{{sfnp|Fukuda|Nihonmatsu|Tokuda|2015|pp=119-123}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|p=147}} The story is here integrated into a medieval legend that claims Suwa Daimyōjin to have originally been [[Takeminakata|a king from India]] who, after performing heroic feats, attained enlightenment and traveled to Japan, where he manifested himself as a local ''kami''. Moriya is identified in this text as an incarnation of the [[Mara (demon)|demon king]] (魔王, ''Maō'') who first antagonized the future Suwa Daimyōjin back in India in the form of a traitorous vassal who fomented a rebellion against the king and then reappeared in Japan as "Moriya the evil outlaw" (洩矢惡賊), where he battled the Suwa deity. After being defeated, Moriya ran away and hid in a mountain behind the Upper Shrine called Moriyagatake (洩矢ヶ嶽, lit. "Moriya's peak"), known today as [[:ja:守屋山|Mount Moriya]] (守屋山, ''Moriya-san''). Moriya, aliased "Yamabe no Moriya" (山家洩矢) and described as the "god's archnemesis" (神明之讎敵, ''shinmei no shūteki''), is compared with Mononobe no Moriya, the "sworn enemy of Buddhism" (佛法之怨敵, ''Buppō no onteki'').{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=150-151}}{{sfnp|Maeda|2019|pp=37-40}} ===="Moriya Daijin" in the ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō''==== [[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|thumb|200px|Suwa Daimyōjin as a warrior in hunting gear]] A document supposedly submitted to the [[Kamakura shogunate]] in 1249 ([[Hōji (era)|Hōji]] 3) by Suwa Nobushige, then ''Ōhōri'' of the Upper Shrine (now considered to be a forgery composed a century later at the earliest{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=50-51}}), known as the ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'' (諏訪信重解状, "The Petition (''Gejō'') of Suwa Nobushige"), features a slightly different version of the myth.''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'' (諏訪信重解状), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻15 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 15)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai |language=ja}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|p=21}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|pp=92-93}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=117-141}} In the petition, Nobushige claimed that "a careful inspection of the ancient customs" revealed that the Upper Shrine stands on what was once land owned by 'Moriya Daijin' (守屋大臣). He then relates a story about how Suwa Daimyōjin came down from heaven to take possession of Moriya Daijin's territory, but the latter would not let him. The dispute between the two eventually escalated into armed conflict, but as no winner could be declared, they competed in a kind of [[tug of war]] using hooks (''kagi'') made out of [[wisteria]] (藤鎰) and iron (鐵鎰), in which the Suwa deity emerged the victor. The triumphant Suwa Daimyōjin then banished Moriya and planted the wisteria ''kagi'' in front of his newly-built dwelling, the future Upper Shrine. The wisteria miraculously turned into a grove known as the "Forest of Fujisuwa" (藤諏訪之森, ''Fujisuwa no mori''), which in turn gave its name to the region.{{efn|「一 守屋山麓御垂跡事
右謹檢舊貫、當砌昔者守屋大臣之所領也、大神天降御之刻、大臣者奉禦明神之居住、勵制止之方法、明神者廻可爲御敷地之祕計。或致諍論、或及合戰之處、兩方難决雌雄、爰明神者持藤鎰、大臣者以鐵鎰、懸此所引之、明神即以藤鎰令勝得軍陣之諍論給、而間令追罰守屋大臣、卜居所當社以來、遙送數百歳星霜、久施我神之稱譽於天下給、應跡之方々是新哉、明神以彼藤鎰自令植當社之前給、藤榮枝葉号藤諏訪之森、毎年二ヶ度御神事勤之、自尓以來以當郡名諏方、爰下宮者當社依夫婦之契約示姫大明神之名、然而當大明神、若不令追出守屋給者、爭兩社卜居御哉、自天降之元初爲本宮之條、炳焉者哉、」}}{{sfnp|Miyaji|1931|p=76}}{{sfnp|Miyaji|1937|pp=47-48}}{{sfnp|Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|1995|pp=811-814}}{{sfnp|Fukuda|Nihonmatsu|Tokuda|2015|pp=121-124}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=153-154}}{{sfnp|Maeda|2019|pp=40-42}} ====In other late medieval texts==== [[File:守屋山 - Mount Moriya.jpg|left|thumb|360x360px|Mount Moriya as seen from Tateishi Park ([[:ja:立石公園 (諏訪市)|立石公園]]) in Suwa City]] The preface of a genealogical record of the Suwa clan thought to date from the 16th century titled the ''Jinshi / Miwa-shi Keizu'' (神氏系図, "Genealogy of the Miwa / Jin Clan"){{sfnp|Miyaji|1931|p=166}}{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|p=88}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=155-156}} states that many conflicting stories concerning the origins of Suwa Daimyōjin exist: the ''[[Kujiki|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'' for instance identifies him as Takeminakata, the son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]], but another legend claims that the Suwa deity first appeared during the time of [[:en:Emperor Yōmei|Emperor Yōmei]] (reigned 585-587). According to this story, Suwa Daimyōjin, accompanied by an eight-year-old boy named [[Takeminakata#The Ōhōri|Arikazu]] (有員), came to Suwa and fought a battle against a certain 'Moriya' (守屋) at Mount Moriya. Moriya was eventually defeated by "divine soldiers" (神兵) led by Arikazu, after which Arikazu established a sanctuary (the Upper Suwa Shrine) on the slopes of the mountain. Suwa Daimyōjin, clothing the boy with his own garments, declared him to be his visible "[[Shintai|body]]" and then disappeared. Suwa Daimyōjin is identified by the story as [[Takeminakata#Under shinbutsu-shūgō|the manifestation]] of the [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]] [[Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]] (Fugen), while Arikazu, who became the founding ancestor of the Suwa clan, is identified with [[Manjushri]] (Monju).{{efn|「神幸信州諏方郡者、人皇卅二代用明天皇御宇也。于時、有八歳童子後字有員而令隨遂明神守屋奉諍。大神至守屋山、有御合戰。童子率神兵、追落守屋。則于彼山麓構社壇。吾神脱着御衣於童子。『吾無躰、以祝爲躰。』有神勅、隱給御身。即彼童子爲神躰、名御衣木祝、神氏始祖也。明神者普賢、童子者文殊也。」}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=155-156}} The same legend is found in another genealogical text titled the'' Miwa-ke / Jinke Keizu'' (神家系図, "Genealogy of the House of Miwa / Jin") or the ''Ōhōri-ke Keizu'' (大祝家系図, "Genealogy of the ''Ōhōri'' House"),{{efn|「用明天皇御宇、大明神影向信濃國諏方郡之時、爲有員童子形体、令御共也。爰同郡守屋大臣奉諍。大明神御來臨之間、至守屋山、彼大臣與大明神在御合戰。于時、有員令御共致合戰、忠追落大臣。則於守屋山麓構社壇、令化現諏訪大明神。即有員始而爲祝奉成祭禮者也。豈大明神者普賢、有員者文殊師利菩薩化身云々。」}}神家系図 (''Jinke Keizu''), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|script-title=ja:諏訪史料叢書 巻28 |title=Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28 |date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/9 |language=ja}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=156-157}} and the ''Ten'in Goroku'' (天陰語録), a [[Muromachi period]] work authored by the [[Rinzai]] monk Ten'in Ryūtaku (天隠龍沢, 1422-1500).{{efn|「神之顯於科野國者。人皇卅二代用明天皇佛法東流之時也。有八歲童子。其名爲有員。隨神以信州也。大臣守屋拒之。童子率兵神以力戰。守屋敗績。弃甲以走。童子追之。就守屋城下。」}}{{cite book|editor1-last=Hanawa|editor1-first=Hokiichi|title=''Ten'in Goroku'' (天陰語録)|date=1914|publisher=Zoku Gunsho-ruijū Kanseikai|series=''[[Gunsho Ruijū|Zoku Gunsho-ruijū]]'' (続群書類従)|volume=13|page=413|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c0Fjxu9FS4EC&pg=PA65 |language=ja|isbn=9784797100631}}{{cite web|title=天隠竜沢|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A9%E9%9A%A0%E7%AB%9C%E6%B2%A2-1093213|website=Kotobank|publisher=Kōdansha, The Asahi Shimbun Company, VOYAGE GROUP, Inc.}} These two works name Suwa Daimyōjin's opponent 'Moriya Daijin' (守屋大臣) or 'Daijin Moriya' (大臣守屋), in agreement with the ''Nobushige Gejō''.{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=156-157}} ====In Edo period texts==== [[File:Lake Suwa 20131231 - panoramio (cropped).jpg|thumb|320x320px|[[Lake Suwa]]]] A ''kōshiki'' from Suwa Shrine surviving in three late 17th century manuscripts titled ''Suwa Kō-no-shiki'' (諏方講之式 / 諏訪講之式) describes Moriya Daijin (守屋大臣) as the [[Tutelary deity|tutelary god]] (地主, ''[[Landlord deity|jinushi]]'' / 地主之靈祇, ''jinushi no reigi'') of Suwa, which was originally named Yamabe (山家[[:wikt:郡#Japanese|郡]], ''Yamabe-[[:en:Districts of Japan|gun]]'' / ''Yamabe no [[:wikt:こおり#Etymology 2|kōri]]''). In order to decide who would gain ownership of the land, Suwa Daimyōjin and Moriya Daijin fought each other using wisteria (藤鑰 / 藤鎰) and iron ''kagi'' (鐵鑰 / 鐵鎰). Suwa Daimyōjin won and planted the wisteria, which eventually became known as Fujishima Myōjin (藤島明神). The name 'Suwa' is claimed here to have originated from Suwa Daimyōjin's exclamation: "Ah (''suwa''{{efn|[[:en:Historical kana orthography|Historical orthography]]: ''suha'' (すは). A cry of amazement, surprise or wonder.{{cite web |title=すは |url=https://kobun.weblio.jp/content/%E3%81%99%E3%81%AF |website=weblio.jp |access-date=2021-10-10}}}}), I have won" (須和吾勝ヌ, ''Suwa ware kachinu'').{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=148-150}} A version of the myth is recounted in a mid-19th century work by merchant and ''[[kokugaku]]'' scholar [[:ja:松沢義章|Matsuzawa Yoshiakira]] (1791-1861), the ''Ken'yū Hongi'' (顕幽本記, "Fundamental Records of the Visible and Invisible [Realms]"). Here, the god Moriya (守屋神, ''Moriya-no-Kami'') is portrayed as the original ruler of Suwa who prevented the "great god" (大御神, ''Ōmikami''; i.e. Suwa Daimyōjin) from entering his domain. In response, the Suwa deity ordered his emissary, Fujishima Daimyōjin (藤島大明神), to subjugate Moriya. Moriya, who was no match for Fujishima Daimyōjin, finally surrendered and went away, allowing Suwa Daimyōjin to take over his land.{{sfnp|Maeda|2019|p=34}} ====In the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu''==== [[File:Moriya Archives museum , 神長官守矢史料館 - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|300px|Entrance to the Moriya family estate and the ''Jinchōkan'' Moriya Historical Museum in Miyagawa, [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City]]]] In the late 19th century, Moriya Saneyoshi (守矢実久), the 76th Moriya clan head and the last person to serve at the Upper Shrine as ''Jinchōkan'' (hereditary priesthood having been abolished by the government in 1871{{sfnp|Inoue|2003|pp=375-376}}{{cite book|last1=Josephson|first1=Jason Ananda|title=The Invention of Religion in Japan|date=2012|publisher=University of Chicago Press|page=150|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gxzuzIszO60C&pg=PA150|isbn=9780226412351}}), compiled a genealogy titled the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜, "Genealogy of the ''Jinchō'' Moriya clan"), which traces the family and their priestly office back to the mythic past.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系図), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|script-title=ja:諏訪史料叢書 巻28 |title=Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24 |language=ja}}{{sfnp|Ōta|1926|pp=15-16}}{{sfnp|Miyaji|1931|p=76}} This text is notable for grafting the ''[[kuni-yuzuri]]'' myth cycle found in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' into the Moriya legend, so that the Suwa deity (Takeminakata) is now portrayed as coming to Suwa [[Takeminakata#Bout_with_Takemikazuchi|after fleeing]] from [[Izumo Province|the land of Izumo]]. {{Quote|'''Moriya-no-Kami (洩矢神)'''
When Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto (御名方刀美命) fled from Izumo to the [[Lake Suwa|sea of Suwa]], the god Moriya who was dwelling by its shores [...] resisted him. Although they fought each other using wisteria and iron hooks (藤鑰鐵鑰), [Moriya] eventually submitted to the august might of Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto and swore: "I give up this land to my lord and [in exchange] will forever take charge of his political and ritual affairs." Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto then recited the following [[Waka (poetry)|song]]: :鹿兒弓乃 眞弓乎持弖 宮滿茂里 矢竹心爾 仕布麻都連與 ([[Man'yōgana]]) :''Kagoyumi no'' / ''mayumi o mochite'' / ''miya mamori'' / ''yatakegokoro ni'' / ''tsukau matsureyo'' :("Wielding your bow / made of [[:en:Euonymus hamiltonianus|spindle wood]], / protect my dwelling (or 'shrine') / and attend to me / stout-heartedly!") He then planted the wisteria [on the ground], which later grew and became known as the Forest of Fujisuwa (藤洲羽森). Together, they then planned to develop the land.{{efn|「洩矢神：御名方刀美命、逃出雲到于洲羽海之時、有洩矢神者居海畔(橋原村社有)拒之、藤國鑰鐵鑰以雖有互相爭事、遂服御名方富命御稜威、誓曰奉乎地永主命之祭政。御名方刀美命歌曰、鹿兒弓乃眞弓乎持弖宮滿茂里矢竹心爾仕布麻都連與。揷彼藤、後繫茂弖曰藤洲羽森。倶謀弖國作。」}}}} ===Other myths=== ====Moriya and Yatsukao / Ganigawara==== [[File:天白七五三社 - Tenpaku-Shime Shrine.jpg|thumb|300px|Tenpaku-Shime Shrine (天白七五三社) in Chinomachi, Chino City]] A story found in a late source claims that Takeminakata and/or Moriya (Moreya) fought another local deity named '''Yatsukao-no-Mikoto''' (矢塚男命), who died during the conflict.{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|p=79}}{{cite web|title=蟹河原 （茅野市ちの横内）|url=http://tateshina-times.jp/?p=7866|website=たてしなの時間|publisher=蓼科企画}} {{Quote|In the history of Tenpaku-Shime Shrine (天白七五三社) in the village of Eimei (永明村, part of modern Chinomachi, Chino), it is said:
An oral tradition relates that the shrine's deity, Yatsukao-no-Mikoto, dwelt in a cave in this area. When Takeminakata-no-Mikoto came to this land, he (Yatsukao?) fought against Moriya-no-Kami using his bow and arrow. When Yatsukao was struck by the arrow and was about to die, he said to Takeminakata-no-Mikoto, "I should have submitted to you, O great god! I entrust my daughter to you." After saying this, he died.''Shinano-no-kuni Kansha Suwa-jinja Jinchōkan Moriya-ke Ryaku-keizu'' (信濃國官社諏訪神社神長官守矢家略系圖), in {{cite book|author1=Nobukawa, Kazuhiko (延川和彦)|author2=Iida, Kotaro (飯田好太郎)|title=諏訪氏系図 続編 (Suwa-shi Keizu, Zokuhen)|date=1921|page=19|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/927368/21}}{{efn|「永明村天白七五三社由緒ニ、字宮渡祭神矢塚男命此地ニ穴居ス、健御名方命此國ニ到リシ時洩矢神ト弓矢を以テ戦フ、矢塚男其矢ニ中リテ死セントシ、建御名方命ニ云フ、我ハ大神ニ随フベシ、一女アリ献ラムト言ヒ終テ死ストノ口傳アリ (下畧)」}}}} A folk version of the story portrays Yatsukao, alias 'Ganigawara no [[:wikt:長者|Chōja]]' (蟹河原の長者), as a chieftain and horse breeder whose might and influence rivaled that of Moreya, one of the powerful chiefs of the region. After Moreya swore fealty to Takeminakata after his defeat, Ganigawara held Moreya in contempt for surrendering to the foreign invader and had servants publicly revile him as a coward. Although their insults went unheeded at first, Ganigawara's men eventually resorted to violence, shooting arrows at the palace Moreya and other deities were erecting for Takeminakata. In retaliation, Takeminakata raised up an army and launched an all-out attack against Ganigawara with Moreya at his side. Ganigawara, mortally wounded by an arrow in the ensuing skirmish, repents in his deathbed and entrusts his youngest daughter to Takeminakata. Takeminakata gives her hand in marriage to a god who was injured by Ganigawara's messengers while guarding his palace.{{sfnp|Imai|1960|pp=42–49}} ====The rain god of Mount Moriya==== [[File:守屋神社奥宮（守屋山東峰） - Mononobe no Moriya Shrine (Mt. Moriya).jpg|thumb|330px|A ''hokora'' (fenced by a barricade) in the eastern peak of Mount Moriya dedicated to the deity 'Moriya Daijin', commonly identified with [[Mononobe no Moriya]]. The ''hokora'' was once the target of ritual desecration by locals whenever rain was needed.]] Behind the Upper Shrine, straddling the border between the cities of Suwa and [[Ina, Nagano|Ina]], stands the 1,650 metre-high{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|p=96}}{{cite web|title=守屋山|url=http://www8.shinmai.co.jp/yama/guide/00063.html|website=信州山岳ガイド|publisher=The Shinano Mainichi Shimbun}} Mount Moriya.{{cite web|title=Suwa Taisha Shrine|url=http://www.japanvisitor.com/japan-temples-shrines/suwa-shrine-nagano|website=Japan Visitor}} On its eastern peak stands a miniature shrine or ''[[hokora]]'' enshrining a deity referred to in old documents as 'Moriya Daijin' (守矢大臣 or 守矢大神). This god is identified with either the Moriya of Suwa legend{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|p=93}} or the deified Mononobe no Moriya, who is worshiped in a shrine on the opposite (southern) side of the mountain, in the town of [[Takatō, Nagano|Takatō]] (part of Ina City). Indeed, the ''hokora'' is considered to be this shrine's ''oku (no) miya'' (奥宮, lit. "inner shrine" or "rear shrine"{{efn|Certain Shinto shrines - especially those dedicated to mountain deities - are composed of two or more sanctuaries, one of which, the ''satomiya'' (里宮, lit. "village shrine"), is located in or near civilization, with the other, the ''okumiya'', being situated in a remote location such as higher up the mountain.{{cite web |last1=Nakayama |first1=Kaoru |title=Yamamiya, Satomiya |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9669 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2021-10-13}}}}).{{sfnp|Hara|2018|pp=133-137}}{{sfnp|Terada|Washio|2010|pp=133-134}} Moriya Daijin is considered to be a [[Weather god|weather deity]] who causes rain to fall when angered.{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|pp=80-81}} Local [[Rainmaking (ritual)|rainmaking rituals]] once involved provoking the god into sending rain by vandalizing the ''hokora'' or throwing it down the mountain side.{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|pp=80-81}} Popular belief holds that rain falls whenever clouds gather around the mountain top.{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|p=96}}{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|pp=80-81}}{{sfnp|Hara|2018|pp=140-141}} A local folk song advises people to prepare to mow the fields whenever the following signs of incoming rain are observed: {{Quote|:於自理皮礼 守矢敞雲乎 巻上而 百舌鳥義智奈哿婆 鎌遠登具倍斯 ([[Man'yōgana]]) :(おじり晴れ 守矢へ雲を 巻き上げて もずぎち鳴かば 鎌をとぐべし) :''Ojiri hare'' / ''Moriya e kumo o'' / ''maki agete'' / ''mozu gichi nakaba'' / ''kama o togu beshi'' :"When the sun at [[Tenryū River|Ojiri]] / pushes clouds / towards (Mount) Moriya / and the [[:en:Bull-headed shrike|shrike]] (''mozu'') chatters / sharpen your sickles."{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|p=96}}{{sfnp|Hara|2018|pp=140-141}}}} ===Offspring=== [[File:Moriya Family Tree (English).png|thumb|450px|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'']] One local tradition identifies Moriya as the father of the god Chikatō ([[:ja:千鹿頭神|千鹿頭神]], also 'Chikato'), an obscure deity worshiped in a handful of shrines in the Suwa basin (specifically the cities of Chino and Suwa) and the neighboring municipalities of [[Tatsuno, Nagano|Tatsuno]] and [[Matsumoto, Nagano|Matsumoto]].{{sfnp|Ogura|1941|pp=56-58}} The ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' meanwhile claims him to have had two children, a daughter named Tamaru-hime (多満留姫) and a son named Moriya ([[:ja:守宅神|守宅神]]).{{efn|「守宅神：生弖有靈異幹力、代父弖負弓矢、從大神遊獵得千鹿。有一男、名之曰千鹿頭神。」}} Tamaru-hime married Izuhayao ([[:ja:出速雄神|出速雄神]]), one of Takeminakata's sons,{{efn|「洩矢神 (...) 有一男一女、女曰多滿留姫、嫁大神御子出速雄神。」}} while the younger Moriya fathered Chikatō, who married Urakohime (宇良古比売命), the goddess of Mount Urako (宇良古山; identified with Chikatō Shrine (千鹿頭神社) in Kanda / Satoyamabe, Matsumoto).{{efn|「千鹿頭社　諏訪郡ノ内鎭座　　有賀　上原
原田　横吹　休戸　　東筑摩郡　神田　林
同地宇良古山ニ鎭座ス往古ハ郡内三十餘村ノ祭神ナリ 后神ヲ宇良古比賣命ト云口碑ニ傳フ由同地ニ命ノ社アリ」}}{{sfnp|Ogura|1941|pp=56-58}}{{cite web |title=Detail of Reference Example (2020-09-04) |url=https://crd.ndl.go.jp/reference/detail?page=ref_view&id=1000294807 |website=Collaborative Reference Database |publisher=National Diet Library |access-date=2021-10-13}} Curiously, the genealogy portrays Moriya's biological bloodline to have ended with Chikatō. Subsequent generations instead trace themselves to Kodamahiko (児玉彦命), Takeminakata's grandson via Katakurabe ([[:ja:片倉辺命|片倉辺命]]), who became the successor to the Moriya legacy as per the will of Takeminakata himself.{{efn|「兒玉彦命：大神御子片倉邊命之御子也。大神之御言之隨、千鹿頭神之跡乎繼弖主祭政。守達神御子、美都多麻比賣神乎娶弖、八櫛神乎生。」}}{{sfnp|Takabe Rekishi Hensan Iinkai|2006|p=31}}{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2018|pp=333-336}} ==Analysis== === Setting === {{multiple image | width = 300 | direction = vertical | image1 = Fujishima_Shrine_(藤島社).png | caption1 = Photograph of the Nakasu Fujishima Shrine before 1937. The shrine was later relocated south of the original site somewhere during the latter half of the 20th century.{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|pp=88-93}} | image3 = Fujishima_Shrine_-_藤島神社_(川岸天竜河畔諏訪明神入諏伝説の地).jpg | caption3 = Fujishima Shrine (藤島神社, ''Fujishima-jinja'') in Misawa, Kawagishi-Kami, [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], on the banks of the [[Tenryū River]] }} As noted above, the story of Moriya being defeated by a wisteria branch / vine or an implement made from the plant is presented in some earlier texts such as the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' as the origin myth of Fujishima (lit. "Wisteria Island") Shrine, one of the auxiliary shrines (''sessha'') of the Upper Suwa Shrine, located a short distance away from the Upper Shrine's main shrine (''Kamisha Honmiya'') in Nakasu, Suwa City. ({{coord|36|00|09|N|138|07|08|E}}) === The Moriya myth and the Upper Shrine's origins === The myth of Takeminakata's defeat of Moriya has long fascinated researchers due to its perceived connection with the enigma of the origin of the Upper Suwa Shrine and the relationship between the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' and the Moriya ''Jinchōkan''. The story has been interpreted either as a mythicization of a conflict between indigenous [[Jōmon period|Jōmon]] [[hunter-gatherers]] of the Suwa region and [[:en:Agrarian society|agrarian]] [[Yayoi period|Yayoi peoples]] who began to settle in the area,{{cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Atsuko|script-title=ja:古社叢の「聖地」の構造（3）─諏訪大社の場合|journal=Journal of Kyoto Seika University|pages=122–123|url=http://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|language=ja}}{{cite AV media|title = 古代史ミステリー 「御柱」～最後の"縄文王国"の謎～ (Kodaishi Mystery. Onbashira: Saigo no Jōmon-ōkoku no nazo)|medium=Documentary|publisher=NHK|location=Japan|date = 2016|url=http://www.nhk.or.jp/docudocu/program/46/2586790/|language=ja}} or between the local clans of Suwa and the expanding [[Yamato state]] somewhere during the 6th to 7th centuries CE ([[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]]).{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|pp=18-22}}{{sfnp|Oh|2011|pp=156-157}} Accordingly, Moreya is believed by some to be a deified indigenous priest-chieftain or clan leader who once held political and religious authority over the Suwa region.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|p=2-3}}{{sfnp|Oh|2011|pp=158-159}} The author [[:ja:大和岩雄|Iwao Ōwa]] (1990) meanwhile theorizes Moreya to be a personification of the guardian nature spirit or [[Mishaguji]] worshipped by the Moriya clan. He further proposes that Moreya/Moriya and Moriya/Morita - Moreya's son in the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' - were originally a single figure later split into two, with the elder Moriya (Moreya) being connected with hunting and the younger Moriya (Morita) being mostly associated with sedentary agriculture.{{sfnp|Ōwa|1990|pp=201-202}} [[File:Mononobe no Moriya.jpg|thumb|120px|[[Mononobe no Moriya]] by [[Kikuchi Yōsai]]]] [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|left|The Jinchōkan-ura Kofun (神長官裏古墳) in the Moriya estate in Chino, Nagano. The 7th century tomb is linked with Mononobe no Moriya's supposed son Takemaro in family lore.]] ===Moreya, the Moriya clan and Mononobe no Moriya=== The similarity between the names of both Moreya/Moriya and the 6th century ''[[Muraji|Ōmuraji]]'' [[Mononobe no Moriya]], who opposed [[Buddhism in Japan#Asuka Period (538 to 710) and Nara Period (710–794)|the introduction of Buddhism to Japan]], had led to a long-standing conflation of the two figures (cf. Moreya being called ''Moriya Daijin'' in medieval texts). A certain legend claims that a son of Mononobe no Moriya, named either '''Takemaro''' (武麿) or '''Otogimi''' (弟君), survived the defeat of the Mononobe in the [[Soga–Mononobe conflict|Battle of Mount Shigi]] in 587 and fled to Suwa, where he married into the ''Jinchō'' Moriya clan; Takemaro is thus reckoned as a clan ancestor in the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu''.{{efn|「武麿 (一云弟君): 三十一代用命天皇御宇 物部守屋大連守屋大臣ハ饒速日命苗裔 尾輿大連ノ子爲國殞身河内國澁川館兒孫逃匿葦原或逃、亡長子雄君入美濃、次子武麿入于信濃洲羽來弖娶神氏女嗣長職。」}} A small [[kofun|mound]] in the Moriya clan's historical estate in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino]] dated to the 7th century{{cite web|title=神長官裏古墳|url=http://kofun.info/kofun/815|website=古墳マップ (Kofun Map)}} is claimed in family lore to be Takemaro's tomb.Moriya (1991). pp. 6-7. Ōwa (1990) believes this story to be modelled after the biography of Mononobe no Masara (物部麻佐良), who according to the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' married Imoko (妹古), the daughter of an unidentified 'Suwa-no-[[Kabane|Atai]]' (須羽直) during the reign of [[:en:Emperor Buretsu|Emperor Buretsu]] in the late 5th century, yet sees it as at least being inspired by a real-life connection between the Mononobe clan and Shinano Province.Ōwa (1990). pp. 110-111. Moriya Shrine in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]] where Moreya is worshipped currently denies any connection between the god and the Mononobe chancellor.{{cite web|title=洩矢神社とは|url=https://moriyajinja.amebaownd.com/pages/738296/page_201611220733|website=洩矢神社公式HP (Moriya Shrine Official Homepage)}} ==Descendants== Moreya is held to be the ancestor of the Moriya clan (守矢氏), which traditionally served as priests of the Suwa ''Kamisha''.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|p=2-3}} The chief priest of the ''Kamisha'' was the ''[[Suwa clan#As ōhōri|ōhōri]]'' or ''ōhafuri'' (大祝 'great priest'), who was considered to be a [[Arahitogami|living deity]] and the embodiment of Suwa Myōjin, the god of the shrine. Assisting the ''ōhōri'' (who by tradition was a member of the [[Suwa clan]], Suwa Myōjin's supposed descendants{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|p=2-3}}) were five priests, at the head of which was the ''kan-no-osa'' (神長, also ''jinchō'') or ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), an office occupied by members of the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' oversaw the ''Kamisha'''s rites and ceremonies in general and summoned [[Mishaguji]] - a god or gods [[:en:Animism|thought to inhabit rocks or trees]] worshipped in the region since ancient timesMoriya (1991), p. 4.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=やおよろず 日本の神様辞典 (Yaorozu - Nihon no kamisama jiten)}} and regarded by the Moriya as their patron deity - to [[Spirit possession|possess]] individuals or inanimate objects during ceremonies, being the only one considered to be able to do so.Miyasaka (1987). p. 22. [[File:Jinchokan Moriya Museum.jpg|thumb|left|200px|The Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino, Nagano]], built by architect [[Terunobu Fujimori]].]]It has been observed that the religious climate of Suwa is a syncretism of ancient indigenous beliefs and practices (e.g. the worship of Mishaguji) reorganized under a Yamato framework (e.g. Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata, the cult of the ''ōhōri''), but with the local element still predominant. Despite (or perhaps because of) his officially being a living god and the ''Kamisha'''s chief priest, the Suwa ''ōhōri'' - who assumed the office during childhood - had little, if any, real power or influence in the shrine's affairs, which firmly rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'',Oh (2011), p. 158. with his unique ability to hear Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon someone or something and his knowledge of special rituals, which were closely guarded secrets traditionally passed down via word of mouth only to a single individual, the heir to the office of ''jinchōkan''.Moriya (1991), p. 5.Miyasaka (1987). p. 27. The establishment of [[State Shinto]] in the [[Meiji period]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priests and private ownership of shrines. Accordingly, the shrine at Suwa passed under the control of the state, with government appointees replacing the clans who had historically served as its priests, the Suwa and the Moriya among them. As the ancient priestly offices of the shrine became defunct, most of the unwritten tradition once guarded by the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' died with the last occupant of the position. A museum dedicated to preserving information about the Moriya and documents owned by the family, the [[:ja:神長官守矢史料館|Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum]] (神長官守矢史料館 ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan''), currently stands on the clan estate in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City, Nagano]].{{cite web|title=神長官守矢資料館|url=http://www.zephyr.dti.ne.jp/bushi/siseki/moriya.htm|website=武田氏の史跡探訪}}{{cite book|last1=Buntrock|first1=Dana|title=Materials and Meaning in Contemporary Japanese Architecture: Tradition and Today|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-134-72501-4|page=17|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eTzcAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA17}} ==Shrine== A single shrine to Moreya, [https://www.google.com/maps/place/%E6%B4%A9%E7%9F%A2%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE/@36.0509086,138.0340072,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m5!3m4!1s0x601cfe2df9abbb03:0x6da6a669d0b38dbc!8m2!3d36.0509043!4d138.0361959 Moriya Shrine] (洩矢神社 ''Moriya-jinja''), stands in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]], [[Nagano Prefecture|Nagano]], near the Tenryū River. On the opposite bank stands [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E8%97%A4%E5%B3%B6%E7%A4%BE/@36.0533034,138.0343004,85m/data=!3m1!1e3!4m5!3m4!1s0x0:0xaa578226f1624a6f!8m2!3d36.0532219!4d138.0343569?hl=en Fujishima Shrine] (藤島神社 ''Fujishima-jinja''), where legend says Suwa Myōjin stood or encamped during the battle. [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E8%97%A4%E5%B3%B6%E7%A4%BE/@36.0026973,138.1168832,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c565f74160f9b:0x2df0d109a200efc8!8m2!3d36.0026922!4d138.1190749 The other Fujishima Shrine] (藤島社 ''Fujishima-sha''), where the wisteria Suwa Myōjin used during the battle was supposedly planted and sprouted, is in Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]].{{cite web|title=藤島社・藤島大明神 諏訪市中洲神宮寺|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/hujisimasya.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}}Miyachi (1992), pp. 91-93. ==See also== *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Mononobe no Moriya]] *[[Suwa Daimyōjin {{Short description|Japanese god}} {{Infobox deity | type = Japanese | name = Moriya-no-Kami
(Moriya) | image = Moriya Shrine - 洩矢神社 社殿.jpg | caption = Moriya Shrine in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], [[Nagano Prefecture]] | god_of = Indigenous ''[[kami]]'' of the [[Lake Suwa]] area | script_name = Japanese | script = 洩矢神, 守矢神, 守屋神, 守宅神 | other_names = Moriya (Moreya)-no-Ōkami (洩矢大神)
Moriya Daimyōjin (守屋大明神)
Moriya Daijin (守屋大臣)
Moriya no Akuzoku (洩矢の悪賊) | cult_center = [[:ja:洩矢神社|Moriya Shrine]] | children = [[:ja:守宅神|Moriya]] / Morita (son; ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'')
Tamaru-hime (daughter; ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'')
[[:ja:千鹿頭神|Chikatō]] (son; local legend) | texts = ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'', ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'', ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' }} '''Moreya''' or '''Moriya''' (洩矢神, ''Moriya- / Moriya'') is a Japanese [[Kami|god]] who appears in various myths and legends of the [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]] region in [[Nagano Prefecture]] (historical [[Shinano Province]]). The most famous of such stories is that of his battle against [[Takeminakata]], the god of the [[Suwa-taisha|Grand Shrine of Suwa]] (''Suwa Taisha''). Moriya is regarded as the mythical ancestor of the Moriya clan (守矢氏), a priestly family that formerly served in the Upper Suwa Shrine (上社, ''Kamisha''), one of the two sub-shrines that make up Suwa Taisha. In addition, he is venerated as a local tutelary deity (''[[Ujigami|ubusunagami]]'') in a shrine in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]] near the [[Tenryū River]], which in later variants of the aforementioned myth is identified as the place where Takeminakata and Moriya fought each other. Local historians have long interpreted the story of the conflict between the two deities as the mythicization of a historical event in which a powerful local clan that ruled the [[Lake Suwa]] region and its vicinity (identified with the Moriya) was defeated by invaders who wrested control of the area (identified in turn with the [[Suwa clan]], the high priestly lineage of the Upper Suwa Shrine that claimed to be Takeminakata's descendants), although a number of scholars have recently argued that it may actually be of later origin, heavily influenced by or outright based on medieval legends concerning [[Soga–Mononobe conflict|the conflict]] between [[Prince Shōtoku]] and the anti-Buddhist ''[[Muraji|ōmuraji]]'' [[Mononobe no Moriya]], who may have been the inspiration for the god's name. ==Name== What is currently the most commonly used rendering of Moriya's name in [[kanji]], 洩矢, appear in sources such as the ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'' (1356) and the genealogical record of the Moriya family compiled during the early [[Meiji period]] (late 19th century) known as the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜, "Genealogy of the ''Jinchō'' Moriya clan"). It is also the rendering adopted by Moriya Shrine ([[:ja:洩矢神社|洩矢神社]]) in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]] in Nagano, where the deity is enshrined.{{cite web|url=https://moriyajinja.amebaownd.com/|title=Moriya Shrine Official Website (洩矢神社公式HP)}} A number of other texts (see below) meanwhile refer to the god as ''Moriya Daijin'' (守屋大臣), an epithet more often used for the historical Mononobe no Moriya in medieval and later sources.''Nihon Kōtei Keizu'' (日本皇帝系図), in {{cite book|editor1=Hanawa Hokiichi|title=群書系図部集 第二 (Gunsho keizubushū, vol. 2)|date=1973|publisher=Zoku Gunsho-ruijū Kanseikai|page=51|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dxv_wsnc14YC&pg=RA1-PA19|isbn=9784797102741}}{{cite book|last1=Dickson|first1=Walter G.|title=Gleanings from Japan|date=1889|publisher=W. Blackwood and Sons|page=[https://archive.org/details/gleaningsfromja01dickgoog/page/n370 360]|url=https://archive.org/details/gleaningsfromja01dickgoog}}{{cite book|last1=Arai|first1=Hakuseki|translator=Joly, Henri L. |translator2=Inada, Hogitarō|title=The Sword Book in Honchō Gunkikō and the Book of Samé Ko Hi Sei Gi of Inaba Tsurio|date=1963|publisher=Charles E. Tuttle|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JWceAAAAIAAJ&q=moriya+daijin|page=14}} ==Background== ===Suwa Shrine and its priesthood=== [[File:Suwa-taisha, Kamisha Honmiya, haiden-2.jpg|thumb|312x312px|The Upper Shrine of Suwa's Main Shrine (上社本宮, ''Kamisha Honmiya''), located in [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]]]] The Grand Shrine of Suwa (''Suwa Taisha'') in [[Nagano Prefecture]] consists of four shrines grouped into two sites: the Upper Shrine (上社, ''Kamisha''), located southeast of [[Lake Suwa]], in the cities of [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino]] and [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa]], and the Lower Shrine (下社, ''Shimosha''), located in the town of [[Shimosuwa]] in the northern side of the lake. Historically, the Upper and Lower Suwa Shrines essentially functioned as two separate entities, each with its own set of shrines, religious ceremonies, and priests. Before the rise of [[State Shinto]] in the [[Meiji period]], the position of head priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝) in the Upper Shrine was occupied by members of the [[Suwa clan]] (諏訪氏, ''Suwa-shi''), also known as the Miwa or Jin (神氏, ''Jinshi'' / ''Miwa-shi''). The Suwa traditionally traced its lineage back to the shrine's deity [[Takeminakata]], who is also known as Suwa [[Myōjin|Daimyōjin]] (諏訪大明神), the "Great Deity of Suwa." For a long time, the occupant of the high priestly office was revered as a god in the flesh (''[[arahitogami]]''), the living incarnation or "body" (''[[shintai]]'') of Suwa Daimyōjin.{{sfnp|Ihara|2008|pp=157–185}}{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|pp=2-3}}{{sfnp|Inoue|2003|pp=356-357}} The second-highest office was that of the ''Kan-no-Osa'' or ''Jinchō'' (神長), later known as the ''Jinchōkan'' (神長官). This priest officiated the Upper Shrine's ceremonies, including the ''Ōhōri'''s investiture ceremony, which accorded him a preeminent status in the hierarchy. He also had the prerogative of summoning and inhering the [[Mishaguji]], divine spirits who figure in some of the shrine's religious rites, onto objects who will serve as their vessels (''[[yorishiro]]'') for the duration of these rituals and then dismissing them at their conclusion.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|pp=4-5}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|pp=25-27}} The hereditary occupants of this office were members of a clan called Moriya (守矢氏, ''Moriya-shi''), who claimed to have descended from a certain local god named Moriya or Moreya, who had been subjugated by Takeminakata.{{sfnp|Inoue|2003|pp=356-357}} ==Mythology== ===Moriya and Suwa Daimyōjin=== The most famous story involving Moriya is that of his battle against Takeminakata / Suwa Daimyōjin, who is said to have come to the Suwa region seeking to dwell there or to conquer it. One version of this myth involves the Suwa deity or his subordinate defeating Moriya, described as armed with a certain kind of iron weapon or implement, using only a [[wisteria]] (藤, ''fuji'') branch or vine.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|pp=2-3}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|p=21}}{{sfnp|Oh|2011|pp=157-158}}{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|pp=24-25}} Another variant has Suwa Daimyōjin facing and defeating Moriya on the battlefield. ==== "Moriya the evil outlaw" in the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' ==== [[File:Fujishima Shrine (Nakasu, Suwa) - 藤島社（諏訪市中洲）- 2.jpg|thumb|353x353px|Fujishima Shrine (藤島社) in Nakasu, Suwa, one of the Upper Shrine of Suwa's [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrines]]]] What is perhaps the most well-known version of the story is found in the 1356 text ''[[Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba]]'', where it is recorded as the [[origin myth]] of Fujishima Shrine (藤島社, ''Fujishima-sha'') in [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]], one of the Upper Shrine's [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrines]] where its yearly rice-planting ceremony is traditionally held.{{sfnp|Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|1995|pp=681-683}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|pp=88-91}} {{Quote|Regarding the god of Fujishima [Shrine] (藤島の明神, ''Fujishima no Myōjin''): when the revered deity (尊神, ''sonjin'', i.e. Suwa Daimyōjin) [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] long ago, Moriya the evil outlaw (洩矢の惡賊, ''Moriya no akuzoku''), seeking to hinder him, took up an iron ring (鐵輪) to fight him, but the [Fujishima] deity picked up a wisteria branch and defeated [Moriya]. Finally, he brought down heresy (邪輪, ''jarin'', lit. "ring/wheel/circle of evil") and held up [[:en:Dharma (Buddhism)|the true Dharma]] (正法, ''shōbō''). When the god swore an oath and threw the wisteria branch away, immediately it took root [in the ground], its branches and leaves flourishing in abundance, and [sprouted] beautiful blossoms, leaving behind a marker of the battleground for posterity. This is the reason why the Fujishima deity is named thus.{{efn|「抑コノ藤嶋ノ明神ト申ハ、尊神垂迹ノ昔、洩矢ノ惡賊神居ヲサマタケントセシ時、洩矢ハ鐵輪ヲ持シテアラソヒ、明神ハ藤枝ヲトリテ是ヲ伏シ給フ。ツイニ邪輪ヲ降シテ正法ヲ興ス。 明神誓ヲ發テ、藤枝ヲナケ給シカハ、則根ヲサシテ枝葉ヲサカヘ、花蘂アサヤカニシテ、戰場ノシルシヲ萬代ニ殘ス。藤嶋ノ明神ト号スル此ユヘナリ。」}}{{sfnp|Kanai|1982|p=252}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=151-152}}}} The myth is also found in a [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinto-Buddhist]] liturgical eulogy (講式, ''kōshiki'') to the Suwa deity, the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki'' (諏方大明神講式), thought to have been composed by the ''Ekotoba'''s author, Suwa (Kosaka) Enchū (1295-1364{{sfnp|Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|1995|p=814}}), around the same time as the former text.{{cite web|title=諏方大明神講式|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=KSRM-287105|website=National Institute of Japanese Literature (国文学研究資料館)}}{{sfnp|Shintō Taikei Hensankai|1982|pp=9, 237ff.}}{{sfnp|Fukuda|Nihonmatsu|Tokuda|2015|pp=119-123}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|p=147}} The story is here integrated into a medieval legend that claims Suwa Daimyōjin to have originally been [[Takeminakata|a king from India]] who, after performing heroic feats, attained enlightenment and traveled to Japan, where he manifested himself as a local ''kami''. Moriya is identified in this text as an incarnation of the [[Mara (demon)|demon king]] (魔王, ''Maō'') who first antagonized the future Suwa Daimyōjin back in India in the form of a traitorous vassal who fomented a rebellion against the king and then reappeared in Japan as "Moriya the evil outlaw" (洩矢惡賊), where he battled the Suwa deity. After being defeated, Moriya ran away and hid in a mountain behind the Upper Shrine called Moriyagatake (洩矢ヶ嶽, lit. "Moriya's peak"), known today as [[:ja:守屋山|Mount Moriya]] (守屋山, ''Moriya-san''). Moriya, aliased "Yamabe no Moriya" (山家洩矢) and described as the "god's archnemesis" (神明之讎敵, ''shinmei no shūteki''), is compared with Mononobe no Moriya, the "sworn enemy of Buddhism" (佛法之怨敵, ''Buppō no onteki'').{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=150-151}}{{sfnp|Maeda|2019|pp=37-40}} ===="Moriya Daijin" in the ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō''==== [[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|thumb|200px|Suwa Daimyōjin as a warrior in hunting gear]] A document supposedly submitted to the [[Kamakura shogunate]] in 1249 ([[Hōji (era)|Hōji]] 3) by Suwa Nobushige, then ''Ōhōri'' of the Upper Shrine (now considered to be a forgery composed a century later at the earliest{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=50-51}}), known as the ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'' (諏訪信重解状, "The Petition (''Gejō'') of Suwa Nobushige"), features a slightly different version of the myth.''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'' (諏訪信重解状), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|title=諏訪史料叢書 巻15 (Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 15)|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai |language=ja}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|p=21}}{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|pp=92-93}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=117-141}} In the petition, Nobushige claimed that "a careful inspection of the ancient customs" revealed that the Upper Shrine stands on what was once land owned by 'Moriya Daijin' (守屋大臣). He then relates a story about how Suwa Daimyōjin came down from heaven to take possession of Moriya Daijin's territory, but the latter would not let him. The dispute between the two eventually escalated into armed conflict, but as no winner could be declared, they competed in a kind of [[tug of war]] using hooks (''kagi'') made out of [[wisteria]] (藤鎰) and iron (鐵鎰), in which the Suwa deity emerged the victor. The triumphant Suwa Daimyōjin then banished Moriya and planted the wisteria ''kagi'' in front of his newly-built dwelling, the future Upper Shrine. The wisteria miraculously turned into a grove known as the "Forest of Fujisuwa" (藤諏訪之森, ''Fujisuwa no mori''), which in turn gave its name to the region.{{efn|「一 守屋山麓御垂跡事
右謹檢舊貫、當砌昔者守屋大臣之所領也、大神天降御之刻、大臣者奉禦明神之居住、勵制止之方法、明神者廻可爲御敷地之祕計。或致諍論、或及合戰之處、兩方難决雌雄、爰明神者持藤鎰、大臣者以鐵鎰、懸此所引之、明神即以藤鎰令勝得軍陣之諍論給、而間令追罰守屋大臣、卜居所當社以來、遙送數百歳星霜、久施我神之稱譽於天下給、應跡之方々是新哉、明神以彼藤鎰自令植當社之前給、藤榮枝葉号藤諏訪之森、毎年二ヶ度御神事勤之、自尓以來以當郡名諏方、爰下宮者當社依夫婦之契約示姫大明神之名、然而當大明神、若不令追出守屋給者、爭兩社卜居御哉、自天降之元初爲本宮之條、炳焉者哉、」}}{{sfnp|Miyaji|1931|p=76}}{{sfnp|Miyaji|1937|pp=47-48}}{{sfnp|Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|1995|pp=811-814}}{{sfnp|Fukuda|Nihonmatsu|Tokuda|2015|pp=121-124}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=153-154}}{{sfnp|Maeda|2019|pp=40-42}} ====In other late medieval texts==== [[File:守屋山 - Mount Moriya.jpg|left|thumb|360x360px|Mount Moriya as seen from Tateishi Park ([[:ja:立石公園 (諏訪市)|立石公園]]) in Suwa City]] The preface of a genealogical record of the Suwa clan thought to date from the 16th century titled the ''Jinshi / Miwa-shi Keizu'' (神氏系図, "Genealogy of the Miwa / Jin Clan"){{sfnp|Miyaji|1931|p=166}}{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|p=88}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=155-156}} states that many conflicting stories concerning the origins of Suwa Daimyōjin exist: the ''[[Kujiki|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'' for instance identifies him as Takeminakata, the son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]], but another legend claims that the Suwa deity first appeared during the time of [[:en:Emperor Yōmei|Emperor Yōmei]] (reigned 585-587). According to this story, Suwa Daimyōjin, accompanied by an eight-year-old boy named [[Takeminakata#The Ōhōri|Arikazu]] (有員), came to Suwa and fought a battle against a certain 'Moriya' (守屋) at Mount Moriya. Moriya was eventually defeated by "divine soldiers" (神兵) led by Arikazu, after which Arikazu established a sanctuary (the Upper Suwa Shrine) on the slopes of the mountain. Suwa Daimyōjin, clothing the boy with his own garments, declared him to be his visible "[[Shintai|body]]" and then disappeared. Suwa Daimyōjin is identified by the story as [[Takeminakata#Under shinbutsu-shūgō|the manifestation]] of the [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]] [[Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]] (Fugen), while Arikazu, who became the founding ancestor of the Suwa clan, is identified with [[Manjushri]] (Monju).{{efn|「神幸信州諏方郡者、人皇卅二代用明天皇御宇也。于時、有八歳童子後字有員而令隨遂明神守屋奉諍。大神至守屋山、有御合戰。童子率神兵、追落守屋。則于彼山麓構社壇。吾神脱着御衣於童子。『吾無躰、以祝爲躰。』有神勅、隱給御身。即彼童子爲神躰、名御衣木祝、神氏始祖也。明神者普賢、童子者文殊也。」}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=155-156}} The same legend is found in another genealogical text titled the'' Miwa-ke / Jinke Keizu'' (神家系図, "Genealogy of the House of Miwa / Jin") or the ''Ōhōri-ke Keizu'' (大祝家系図, "Genealogy of the ''Ōhōri'' House"),{{efn|「用明天皇御宇、大明神影向信濃國諏方郡之時、爲有員童子形体、令御共也。爰同郡守屋大臣奉諍。大明神御來臨之間、至守屋山、彼大臣與大明神在御合戰。于時、有員令御共致合戰、忠追落大臣。則於守屋山麓構社壇、令化現諏訪大明神。即有員始而爲祝奉成祭禮者也。豈大明神者普賢、有員者文殊師利菩薩化身云々。」}}神家系図 (''Jinke Keizu''), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|script-title=ja:諏訪史料叢書 巻28 |title=Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28 |date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/9 |language=ja}}{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=156-157}} and the ''Ten'in Goroku'' (天陰語録), a [[Muromachi period]] work authored by the [[Rinzai]] monk Ten'in Ryūtaku (天隠龍沢, 1422-1500).{{efn|「神之顯於科野國者。人皇卅二代用明天皇佛法東流之時也。有八歲童子。其名爲有員。隨神以信州也。大臣守屋拒之。童子率兵神以力戰。守屋敗績。弃甲以走。童子追之。就守屋城下。」}}{{cite book|editor1-last=Hanawa|editor1-first=Hokiichi|title=''Ten'in Goroku'' (天陰語録)|date=1914|publisher=Zoku Gunsho-ruijū Kanseikai|series=''[[Gunsho Ruijū|Zoku Gunsho-ruijū]]'' (続群書類従)|volume=13|page=413|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c0Fjxu9FS4EC&pg=PA65 |language=ja|isbn=9784797100631}}{{cite web|title=天隠竜沢|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A9%E9%9A%A0%E7%AB%9C%E6%B2%A2-1093213|website=Kotobank|publisher=Kōdansha, The Asahi Shimbun Company, VOYAGE GROUP, Inc.}} These two works name Suwa Daimyōjin's opponent 'Moriya Daijin' (守屋大臣) or 'Daijin Moriya' (大臣守屋), in agreement with the ''Nobushige Gejō''.{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=156-157}} ====In Edo period texts==== [[File:Lake Suwa 20131231 - panoramio (cropped).jpg|thumb|320x320px|[[Lake Suwa]]]] A ''kōshiki'' from Suwa Shrine surviving in three late 17th century manuscripts titled ''Suwa Kō-no-shiki'' (諏方講之式 / 諏訪講之式) describes Moriya Daijin (守屋大臣) as the [[Tutelary deity|tutelary god]] (地主, ''[[Landlord deity|jinushi]]'' / 地主之靈祇, ''jinushi no reigi'') of Suwa, which was originally named Yamabe (山家[[:wikt:郡#Japanese|郡]], ''Yamabe-[[:en:Districts of Japan|gun]]'' / ''Yamabe no [[:wikt:こおり#Etymology 2|kōri]]''). In order to decide who would gain ownership of the land, Suwa Daimyōjin and Moriya Daijin fought each other using wisteria (藤鑰 / 藤鎰) and iron ''kagi'' (鐵鑰 / 鐵鎰). Suwa Daimyōjin won and planted the wisteria, which eventually became known as Fujishima Myōjin (藤島明神). The name 'Suwa' is claimed here to have originated from Suwa Daimyōjin's exclamation: "Ah (''suwa''{{efn|[[:en:Historical kana orthography|Historical orthography]]: ''suha'' (すは). A cry of amazement, surprise or wonder.{{cite web |title=すは |url=https://kobun.weblio.jp/content/%E3%81%99%E3%81%AF |website=weblio.jp |access-date=2021-10-10}}}}), I have won" (須和吾勝ヌ, ''Suwa ware kachinu'').{{sfnp|Nihonmatsu|2019|pp=148-150}} A version of the myth is recounted in a mid-19th century work by merchant and ''[[kokugaku]]'' scholar [[:ja:松沢義章|Matsuzawa Yoshiakira]] (1791-1861), the ''Ken'yū Hongi'' (顕幽本記, "Fundamental Records of the Visible and Invisible [Realms]"). Here, the god Moriya (守屋神, ''Moriya-no-Kami'') is portrayed as the original ruler of Suwa who prevented the "great god" (大御神, ''Ōmikami''; i.e. Suwa Daimyōjin) from entering his domain. In response, the Suwa deity ordered his emissary, Fujishima Daimyōjin (藤島大明神), to subjugate Moriya. Moriya, who was no match for Fujishima Daimyōjin, finally surrendered and went away, allowing Suwa Daimyōjin to take over his land.{{sfnp|Maeda|2019|p=34}} ====In the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu''==== [[File:Moriya Archives museum , 神長官守矢史料館 - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|300px|Entrance to the Moriya family estate and the ''Jinchōkan'' Moriya Historical Museum in Miyagawa, [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City]]]] In the late 19th century, Moriya Saneyoshi (守矢実久), the 76th Moriya clan head and the last person to serve at the Upper Shrine as ''Jinchōkan'' (hereditary priesthood having been abolished by the government in 1871{{sfnp|Inoue|2003|pp=375-376}}{{cite book|last1=Josephson|first1=Jason Ananda|title=The Invention of Religion in Japan|date=2012|publisher=University of Chicago Press|page=150|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gxzuzIszO60C&pg=PA150|isbn=9780226412351}}), compiled a genealogy titled the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系譜, "Genealogy of the ''Jinchō'' Moriya clan"), which traces the family and their priestly office back to the mythic past.''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' (神長守矢氏系図), in {{cite book|editor=Suwa Kyōikukai (諏訪教育会)|script-title=ja:諏訪史料叢書 巻28 |title=Suwa shiryō-sōsho, vol. 28|date=1931|location=Suwa|publisher=Suwa Kyōikukai|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185913/24 |language=ja}}{{sfnp|Ōta|1926|pp=15-16}}{{sfnp|Miyaji|1931|p=76}} This text is notable for grafting the ''[[kuni-yuzuri]]'' myth cycle found in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' into the Moriya legend, so that the Suwa deity (Takeminakata) is now portrayed as coming to Suwa [[Takeminakata#Bout_with_Takemikazuchi|after fleeing]] from [[Izumo Province|the land of Izumo]]. {{Quote|'''Moriya-no-Kami (洩矢神)'''
When Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto (御名方刀美命) fled from Izumo to the [[Lake Suwa|sea of Suwa]], the god Moriya who was dwelling by its shores [...] resisted him. Although they fought each other using wisteria and iron hooks (藤鑰鐵鑰), [Moriya] eventually submitted to the august might of Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto and swore: "I give up this land to my lord and [in exchange] will forever take charge of his political and ritual affairs." Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto then recited the following [[Waka (poetry)|song]]: :鹿兒弓乃 眞弓乎持弖 宮滿茂里 矢竹心爾 仕布麻都連與 ([[Man'yōgana]]) :''Kagoyumi no'' / ''mayumi o mochite'' / ''miya mamori'' / ''yatakegokoro ni'' / ''tsukau matsureyo'' :("Wielding your bow / made of [[:en:Euonymus hamiltonianus|spindle wood]], / protect my dwelling (or 'shrine') / and attend to me / stout-heartedly!") He then planted the wisteria [on the ground], which later grew and became known as the Forest of Fujisuwa (藤洲羽森). Together, they then planned to develop the land.{{efn|「洩矢神：御名方刀美命、逃出雲到于洲羽海之時、有洩矢神者居海畔(橋原村社有)拒之、藤國鑰鐵鑰以雖有互相爭事、遂服御名方富命御稜威、誓曰奉乎地永主命之祭政。御名方刀美命歌曰、鹿兒弓乃眞弓乎持弖宮滿茂里矢竹心爾仕布麻都連與。揷彼藤、後繫茂弖曰藤洲羽森。倶謀弖國作。」}}}} ===Other myths=== ====Moriya and Yatsukao / Ganigawara==== [[File:天白七五三社 - Tenpaku-Shime Shrine.jpg|thumb|300px|Tenpaku-Shime Shrine (天白七五三社) in Chinomachi, Chino City]] A story found in a late source claims that Takeminakata and/or Moriya (Moreya) fought another local deity named '''Yatsukao-no-Mikoto''' (矢塚男命), who died during the conflict.{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|p=79}}{{cite web|title=蟹河原 （茅野市ちの横内）|url=http://tateshina-times.jp/?p=7866|website=たてしなの時間|publisher=蓼科企画}} {{Quote|In the history of Tenpaku-Shime Shrine (天白七五三社) in the village of Eimei (永明村, part of modern Chinomachi, Chino), it is said:
An oral tradition relates that the shrine's deity, Yatsukao-no-Mikoto, dwelt in a cave in this area. When Takeminakata-no-Mikoto came to this land, he (Yatsukao?) fought against Moriya-no-Kami using his bow and arrow. When Yatsukao was struck by the arrow and was about to die, he said to Takeminakata-no-Mikoto, "I should have submitted to you, O great god! I entrust my daughter to you." After saying this, he died.''Shinano-no-kuni Kansha Suwa-jinja Jinchōkan Moriya-ke Ryaku-keizu'' (信濃國官社諏訪神社神長官守矢家略系圖), in {{cite book|author1=Nobukawa, Kazuhiko (延川和彦)|author2=Iida, Kotaro (飯田好太郎)|title=諏訪氏系図 続編 (Suwa-shi Keizu, Zokuhen)|date=1921|page=19|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/927368/21}}{{efn|「永明村天白七五三社由緒ニ、字宮渡祭神矢塚男命此地ニ穴居ス、健御名方命此國ニ到リシ時洩矢神ト弓矢を以テ戦フ、矢塚男其矢ニ中リテ死セントシ、建御名方命ニ云フ、我ハ大神ニ随フベシ、一女アリ献ラムト言ヒ終テ死ストノ口傳アリ (下畧)」}}}} A folk version of the story portrays Yatsukao, alias 'Ganigawara no [[:wikt:長者|Chōja]]' (蟹河原の長者), as a chieftain and horse breeder whose might and influence rivaled that of Moreya, one of the powerful chiefs of the region. After Moreya swore fealty to Takeminakata after his defeat, Ganigawara held Moreya in contempt for surrendering to the foreign invader and had servants publicly revile him as a coward. Although their insults went unheeded at first, Ganigawara's men eventually resorted to violence, shooting arrows at the palace Moreya and other deities were erecting for Takeminakata. In retaliation, Takeminakata raised up an army and launched an all-out attack against Ganigawara with Moreya at his side. Ganigawara, mortally wounded by an arrow in the ensuing skirmish, repents in his deathbed and entrusts his youngest daughter to Takeminakata. Takeminakata gives her hand in marriage to a god who was injured by Ganigawara's messengers while guarding his palace.{{sfnp|Imai|1960|pp=42–49}} ====The rain god of Mount Moriya==== [[File:守屋神社奥宮（守屋山東峰） - Mononobe no Moriya Shrine (Mt. Moriya).jpg|thumb|330px|A ''hokora'' (fenced by a barricade) in the eastern peak of Mount Moriya dedicated to the deity 'Moriya Daijin', commonly identified with [[Mononobe no Moriya]]. The ''hokora'' was once the target of ritual desecration by locals whenever rain was needed.]] Behind the Upper Shrine, straddling the border between the cities of Suwa and [[Ina, Nagano|Ina]], stands the 1,650 metre-high{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|p=96}}{{cite web|title=守屋山|url=http://www8.shinmai.co.jp/yama/guide/00063.html|website=信州山岳ガイド|publisher=The Shinano Mainichi Shimbun}} Mount Moriya.{{cite web|title=Suwa Taisha Shrine|url=http://www.japanvisitor.com/japan-temples-shrines/suwa-shrine-nagano|website=Japan Visitor}} On its eastern peak stands a miniature shrine or ''[[:en:Hokora|Hokora]]'' enshrining a deity referred to in old documents as 'Moriya Daijin' (守矢大臣 or 守矢大神). This god is identified with either the Moriya of Suwa legend{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|p=93}} or the deified Mononobe no Moriya, who is worshiped in a shrine on the opposite (southern) side of the mountain, in the town of [[Takatō, Nagano|Takatō]] (part of Ina City). Indeed, the ''hokora'' is considered to be this shrine's ''oku (no) miya'' (奥宮, lit. "inner shrine" or "rear shrine"{{efn|Certain Shinto shrines - especially those dedicated to mountain deities - are composed of two or more sanctuaries, one of which, the ''satomiya'' (里宮, lit. "village shrine"), is located in or near civilization, with the other, the ''okumiya'', being situated in a remote location such as higher up the mountain.{{cite web |last1=Nakayama |first1=Kaoru |title=Yamamiya, Satomiya |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9669 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2021-10-13}}}}).{{sfnp|Hara|2018|pp=133-137}}{{sfnp|Terada|Washio|2010|pp=133-134}} Moriya Daijin is considered to be a [[Weather god|weather deity]] who causes rain to fall when angered.{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|pp=80-81}} Local [[Rainmaking (ritual)|rainmaking rituals]] once involved provoking the god into sending rain by vandalizing the ''hokora'' or throwing it down the mountain side.{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|pp=80-81}} Popular belief holds that rain falls whenever clouds gather around the mountain top.{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|p=96}}{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2017b|pp=80-81}}{{sfnp|Hara|2018|pp=140-141}} A local folk song advises people to prepare to mow the fields whenever the following signs of incoming rain are observed: {{Quote|:於自理皮礼 守矢敞雲乎 巻上而 百舌鳥義智奈哿婆 鎌遠登具倍斯 ([[Man'yōgana]]) :(おじり晴れ 守矢へ雲を 巻き上げて もずぎち鳴かば 鎌をとぐべし) :''Ojiri hare'' / ''Moriya e kumo o'' / ''maki agete'' / ''mozu gichi nakaba'' / ''kama o togu beshi'' :"When the sun at [[Tenryū River|Ojiri]] / pushes clouds / towards (Mount) Moriya / and the [[:en:Bull-headed shrike|shrike]] (''mozu'') chatters / sharpen your sickles."{{sfnp|Yazaki|1986|p=96}}{{sfnp|Hara|2018|pp=140-141}}}} ===Offspring=== [[File:Moriya Family Tree (English).png|thumb|450px|The first five generations of the Moriya clan according to the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'']] One local tradition identifies Moriya as the father of the god Chikatō ([[:ja:千鹿頭神|千鹿頭神]], also 'Chikato'), an obscure deity worshiped in a handful of shrines in the Suwa basin (specifically the cities of Chino and Suwa) and the neighboring municipalities of [[Tatsuno, Nagano|Tatsuno]] and [[Matsumoto, Nagano|Matsumoto]].{{sfnp|Ogura|1941|pp=56-58}} The ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' meanwhile claims him to have had two children, a daughter named Tamaru-hime (多満留姫) and a son named Moriya ([[:ja:守宅神|守宅神]]).{{efn|「守宅神：生弖有靈異幹力、代父弖負弓矢、從大神遊獵得千鹿。有一男、名之曰千鹿頭神。」}} Tamaru-hime married Izuhayao ([[:ja:出速雄神|出速雄神]]), one of Takeminakata's sons,{{efn|「洩矢神 (...) 有一男一女、女曰多滿留姫、嫁大神御子出速雄神。」}} while the younger Moriya fathered Chikatō, who married Urakohime (宇良古比売命), the goddess of Mount Urako (宇良古山; identified with Chikatō Shrine (千鹿頭神社) in Kanda / Satoyamabe, Matsumoto).{{efn|「千鹿頭社　諏訪郡ノ内鎭座　　有賀　上原
原田　横吹　休戸　　東筑摩郡　神田　林
同地宇良古山ニ鎭座ス往古ハ郡内三十餘村ノ祭神ナリ 后神ヲ宇良古比賣命ト云口碑ニ傳フ由同地ニ命ノ社アリ」}}{{sfnp|Ogura|1941|pp=56-58}}{{cite web |title=Detail of Reference Example (2020-09-04) |url=https://crd.ndl.go.jp/reference/detail?page=ref_view&id=1000294807 |website=Collaborative Reference Database |publisher=National Diet Library |access-date=2021-10-13}} Curiously, the genealogy portrays Moriya's biological bloodline to have ended with Chikatō. Subsequent generations instead trace themselves to Kodamahiko (児玉彦命), Takeminakata's grandson via Katakurabe ([[:ja:片倉辺命|片倉辺命]]), who became the successor to the Moriya legacy as per the will of Takeminakata himself.{{efn|「兒玉彦命：大神御子片倉邊命之御子也。大神之御言之隨、千鹿頭神之跡乎繼弖主祭政。守達神御子、美都多麻比賣神乎娶弖、八櫛神乎生。」}}{{sfnp|Takabe Rekishi Hensan Iinkai|2006|p=31}}{{sfnp|Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai|2018|pp=333-336}} ==Analysis== === Setting === {{multiple image | width = 300 | direction = vertical | image1 = Fujishima_Shrine_(藤島社).png | caption1 = Photograph of the Nakasu Fujishima Shrine before 1937. The shrine was later relocated south of the original site somewhere during the latter half of the 20th century.{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1992|pp=88-93}} | image3 = Fujishima_Shrine_-_藤島神社_(川岸天竜河畔諏訪明神入諏伝説の地).jpg | caption3 = Fujishima Shrine (藤島神社, ''Fujishima-jinja'') in Misawa, Kawagishi-Kami, [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya]], on the banks of the [[Tenryū River]] }} As noted above, the story of Moriya being defeated by a wisteria branch / vine or an implement made from the plant is presented in some earlier texts such as the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' as the origin myth of Fujishima (lit. "Wisteria Island") Shrine, one of the auxiliary shrines (''sessha'') of the Upper Suwa Shrine, located a short distance away from the Upper Shrine's main shrine (''Kamisha Honmiya'') in Nakasu, Suwa City. ({{coord|36|00|09|N|138|07|08|E}}) === The Moriya myth and the Upper Shrine's origins === The myth of Takeminakata's defeat of Moriya has long fascinated researchers due to its perceived connection with the enigma of the origin of the Upper Suwa Shrine and the relationship between the Suwa ''Ōhōri'' and the Moriya ''Jinchōkan''. The story has been interpreted either as a mythicization of a conflict between indigenous [[Jōmon period|Jōmon]] [[hunter-gatherers]] of the Suwa region and [[:en:Agrarian society|agrarian]] [[Yayoi period|Yayoi peoples]] who began to settle in the area,{{cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Atsuko|script-title=ja:古社叢の「聖地」の構造（3）─諏訪大社の場合|journal=Journal of Kyoto Seika University|pages=122–123|url=http://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|language=ja}}{{cite AV media|title = 古代史ミステリー 「御柱」～最後の"縄文王国"の謎～ (Kodaishi Mystery. Onbashira: Saigo no Jōmon-ōkoku no nazo)|medium=Documentary|publisher=NHK|location=Japan|date = 2016|url=http://www.nhk.or.jp/docudocu/program/46/2586790/|language=ja}} or between the local clans of Suwa and the expanding [[Yamato state]] somewhere during the 6th to 7th centuries CE ([[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]]).{{sfnp|Miyasaka|1987|pp=18-22}}{{sfnp|Oh|2011|pp=156-157}} Accordingly, Moreya is believed by some to be a deified indigenous priest-chieftain or clan leader who once held political and religious authority over the Suwa region.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|p=2-3}}{{sfnp|Oh|2011|pp=158-159}} The author [[:ja:大和岩雄|Iwao Ōwa]] (1990) meanwhile theorizes Moreya to be a personification of the guardian nature spirit or [[Mishaguji]] worshipped by the Moriya clan. He further proposes that Moreya/Moriya and Moriya/Morita - Moreya's son in the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu'' - were originally a single figure later split into two, with the elder Moriya (Moreya) being connected with hunting and the younger Moriya (Morita) being mostly associated with sedentary agriculture.{{sfnp|Ōwa|1990|pp=201-202}} [[File:Mononobe no Moriya.jpg|thumb|120px|[[Mononobe no Moriya]] by [[Kikuchi Yōsai]]]] [[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan Jinchoukan-ura-kofun.JPG|thumb|left|The Jinchōkan-ura Kofun (神長官裏古墳) in the Moriya estate in Chino, Nagano. The 7th century tomb is linked with Mononobe no Moriya's supposed son Takemaro in family lore.]] ===Moreya, the Moriya clan and Mononobe no Moriya=== The similarity between the names of both Moreya/Moriya and the 6th century ''[[Muraji|Ōmuraji]]'' [[Mononobe no Moriya]], who opposed [[Buddhism in Japan#Asuka Period (538 to 710) and Nara Period (710–794)|the introduction of Buddhism to Japan]], had led to a long-standing conflation of the two figures (cf. Moreya being called ''Moriya Daijin'' in medieval texts). A certain legend claims that a son of Mononobe no Moriya, named either '''Takemaro''' (武麿) or '''Otogimi''' (弟君), survived the defeat of the Mononobe in the [[Soga–Mononobe conflict|Battle of Mount Shigi]] in 587 and fled to Suwa, where he married into the ''Jinchō'' Moriya clan; Takemaro is thus reckoned as a clan ancestor in the ''Jinchō Moriya-shi Keifu''.{{efn|「武麿 (一云弟君): 三十一代用命天皇御宇 物部守屋大連守屋大臣ハ饒速日命苗裔 尾輿大連ノ子爲國殞身河内國澁川館兒孫逃匿葦原或逃、亡長子雄君入美濃、次子武麿入于信濃洲羽來弖娶神氏女嗣長職。」}} A small [[kofun|mound]] in the Moriya clan's historical estate in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino]] dated to the 7th century{{cite web|title=神長官裏古墳|url=http://kofun.info/kofun/815|website=古墳マップ (Kofun Map)}} is claimed in family lore to be Takemaro's tomb.Moriya (1991). pp. 6-7. Ōwa (1990) believes this story to be modelled after the biography of Mononobe no Masara (物部麻佐良), who according to the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' married Imoko (妹古), the daughter of an unidentified 'Suwa-no-[[Kabane|Atai]]' (須羽直) during the reign of [[:en:Emperor Buretsu|Emperor Buretsu]] in the late 5th century, yet sees it as at least being inspired by a real-life connection between the Mononobe clan and Shinano Province.Ōwa (1990). pp. 110-111. Moriya Shrine in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]] where Moreya is worshipped currently denies any connection between the god and the Mononobe chancellor.{{cite web|title=洩矢神社とは|url=https://moriyajinja.amebaownd.com/pages/738296/page_201611220733|website=洩矢神社公式HP (Moriya Shrine Official Homepage)}} ==Descendants== Moreya is held to be the ancestor of the Moriya clan (守矢氏), which traditionally served as priests of the Suwa ''Kamisha''.{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|p=2-3}} The chief priest of the ''Kamisha'' was the ''[[Suwa clan#As ōhōri|ōhōri]]'' or ''ōhafuri'' (大祝 'great priest'), who was considered to be a [[Arahitogami|living deity]] and the embodiment of Suwa Myōjin, the god of the shrine. Assisting the ''ōhōri'' (who by tradition was a member of the [[Suwa clan]], Suwa Myōjin's supposed descendants{{sfnp|Moriya|1991|p=2-3}}) were five priests, at the head of which was the ''kan-no-osa'' (神長, also ''jinchō'') or ''jinchōkan'' (神長官), an office occupied by members of the Moriya clan. The ''jinchōkan'' oversaw the ''Kamisha'''s rites and ceremonies in general and summoned [[Mishaguji]] - a god or gods [[:en:Animism|thought to inhabit rocks or trees]] worshipped in the region since ancient timesMoriya (1991), p. 4.{{cite web|title=ミシャグジ (Mishaguji)|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E3%83%9F%E3%82%B7%E3%83%A3%E3%82%B0%E3%82%B8.html|website=やおよろず 日本の神様辞典 (Yaorozu - Nihon no kamisama jiten)}} and regarded by the Moriya as their patron deity - to [[Spirit possession|possess]] individuals or inanimate objects during ceremonies, being the only one considered to be able to do so.Miyasaka (1987). p. 22. [[File:Jinchokan Moriya Museum.jpg|thumb|left|200px|The Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino, Nagano]], built by architect [[Terunobu Fujimori]].]]It has been observed that the religious climate of Suwa is a syncretism of ancient indigenous beliefs and practices (e.g. the worship of Mishaguji) reorganized under a Yamato framework (e.g. Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata, the cult of the ''ōhōri''), but with the local element still predominant. Despite (or perhaps because of) his officially being a living god and the ''Kamisha'''s chief priest, the Suwa ''ōhōri'' - who assumed the office during childhood - had little, if any, real power or influence in the shrine's affairs, which firmly rested in the hands of the Moriya ''jinchōkan'',Oh (2011), p. 158. with his unique ability to hear Mishaguji and call upon the god(s) to descend upon someone or something and his knowledge of special rituals, which were closely guarded secrets traditionally passed down via word of mouth only to a single individual, the heir to the office of ''jinchōkan''.Moriya (1991), p. 5.Miyasaka (1987). p. 27. The establishment of [[State Shinto]] in the [[Meiji period]] abolished the tradition of hereditary succession among Shinto priests and private ownership of shrines. Accordingly, the shrine at Suwa passed under the control of the state, with government appointees replacing the clans who had historically served as its priests, the Suwa and the Moriya among them. As the ancient priestly offices of the shrine became defunct, most of the unwritten tradition once guarded by the Moriya ''jinchōkan'' died with the last occupant of the position. A museum dedicated to preserving information about the Moriya and documents owned by the family, the [[:ja:神長官守矢史料館|Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum]] (神長官守矢史料館 ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan''), currently stands on the clan estate in [[:en:Chino, Nagano|Chino City, Nagano]].{{cite web|title=神長官守矢資料館|url=http://www.zephyr.dti.ne.jp/bushi/siseki/moriya.htm|website=武田氏の史跡探訪}}{{cite book|last1=Buntrock|first1=Dana|title=Materials and Meaning in Contemporary Japanese Architecture: Tradition and Today|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-134-72501-4|page=17|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eTzcAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA17}} ==Shrine== A single shrine to Moreya, [https://www.google.com/maps/place/%E6%B4%A9%E7%9F%A2%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE/@36.0509086,138.0340072,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m5!3m4!1s0x601cfe2df9abbb03:0x6da6a669d0b38dbc!8m2!3d36.0509043!4d138.0361959 Moriya Shrine] (洩矢神社 ''Moriya-jinja''), stands in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya City]], [[Nagano Prefecture|Nagano]], near the Tenryū River. On the opposite bank stands [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E8%97%A4%E5%B3%B6%E7%A4%BE/@36.0533034,138.0343004,85m/data=!3m1!1e3!4m5!3m4!1s0x0:0xaa578226f1624a6f!8m2!3d36.0532219!4d138.0343569?hl=en Fujishima Shrine] (藤島神社 ''Fujishima-jinja''), where legend says Suwa Myōjin stood or encamped during the battle. [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92392-0015+Nagano-ken,+Suwa-shi,+Nakasu,+%E8%97%A4%E5%B3%B6%E7%A4%BE/@36.0026973,138.1168832,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m5!3m4!1s0x601c565f74160f9b:0x2df0d109a200efc8!8m2!3d36.0026922!4d138.1190749 The other Fujishima Shrine] (藤島社 ''Fujishima-sha''), where the wisteria Suwa Myōjin used during the battle was supposedly planted and sprouted, is in Nakasu, [[Suwa, Nagano|Suwa City]].{{cite web|title=藤島社・藤島大明神 諏訪市中洲神宮寺|url=http://yatsu-genjin.jp/suwataisya/sanpo/hujisimasya.htm|website=八ヶ岳原人}}Miyachi (1992), pp. 91-93. ==See also== *[[Mishaguji]] *[[Mononobe no Moriya]] *[[Suwa Daimyōjin
